newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Pemex reports higher revenue on oil prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pemex reports higher revenue on oil prices.

text.p: Higher world crude oil prices and demand should bring Mexico's state-owned Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) an unexpected $2 billion in 1996, the oil company's chairman Adrian Lajous said Wednesday.
"There is no doubt that Pemex's results have been favorably affected by prices," Lajous told a news conference.
"At the end of the year I am sure we shall be able to inform you of a...substantial increase, and I am sure it will be of more than $2 billion," Lajous said.

Pemex saw profits before taxes for the first nine months of 1996 improve to $15.651 billion, up 25 percent from the same period a year ago. Third-quarter pre-tax profits were up 34 percent from the same period a year ago to $5.593 billion.
Prices of Pemex Olmeca, Maya and Istmo crudes have risen an average 15 percent to date this year.
"In general terms, I would say that the (world) market atmosphere is one of austerity, one of scarcity and one of high prices," Lajous said.
He said world crude prices should remain at current levels through the end of the year and possibly through mid-1997.

Pemex crude oil production has risen to meet the demand, at 2.855 million bpd in the third quarter, with output expected to rise to a three-year high of 2.883 million bpd in the last three months of 1996, Lajous said.

In turn, crude oil exports rose to 1.53 million bpd in the third quarter, up 5.5 percent from the year-ago period, Pemex said. Crude shipments in the first nine months of 1996 increased to 1.54 million bpd, a 14.9 percent increase from the same period in 1995.
Lajous said the unexpected $2 billion in revenue would help pay for an aggressive investment program totalling $5.916 billion in 1997.

"This increase is very important and will be in part financed by savings from 1996 and unexpected additional income," Lajous said, adding Pemex will also look for capital on the international markets for 1997 budget expenses.
The 67 percent spending increase in dollar terms will focus on improved exploration, he added, with 1997 investment in exploration and production alone scheduled to leap 75 percent to $4.069 billion.

Pemex' proposed 1997 budget -- set to be presented next week for the Chamber of Deputies' approval -- also includes a 46 percent increase in refining activity to $1.375 billion and a 38 percent rise in natural gas spending, not including spending to rebuild the Cactus plants destroyed in an August explosion.
Lajous said spending in the company's petrochemical unit is expected to increase 160 percent to $117 million, a figure he said excluded the expected private investment in petrochemical plants.
Defending the profitability of the plants on the auction block, Lajous acknowledged Pemex could have invested more in their upkeep but denied it was seeking to hand off "junk."
Mexico recently changed its privatization guidelines to auction off only a minority 49 percent stake in the petrochemical industry.
The divestment of Pemex assets will end with the petrochemical sale, which would allow the company to focus on oil and gas production, he said.
